name: ANA Holdings
desc: Japanese airline group that owns All Nippon Airways and low-cost carrier Peach, flying passengers and cargo domestically and internationally.
markets: Japanese domestic network plus international routes to Asia, North America, Europe and Oceania; Star Alliance member.
rationale: Strong Japanese consumer brand with long-haul routes; Japanese Grand Prix at Suzuka and premium travel offer suit hospitality and brand campaigns.

name: Mecachrome
desc: French precision engineering group making machined parts and assemblies for aerospace, motorsport, energy and defence customers.
markets: Aerospace and motorsport customers in Europe and North America; supplies engines for FIA Formula 2 and Formula 3.
rationale: Motorsport engine builder with B2B aerospace customers; F1 technical association could showcase engineering, though budget for sponsorship is limited.

name: Macquarie Group
desc: Australian financial group providing asset management, infrastructure investment, banking, commodities trading and corporate advisory services.
industry: diversified investment bank and asset manager
markets: Operates in about 34 markets across Australia, the Americas, Europe and Asia; retail banking mainly in Australia.
rationale: Global institutional client base suits F1 B2B hospitality; Australian retail brand could use the Melbourne race; rival banks already sponsor F1.

name: voestalpine
desc: Austrian steel and technology group making specialty steel, tool steel, rail systems and formed metal parts for industrial customers.
markets: Production and sales companies in about 50 countries, supplying automotive, aerospace, rail and energy customers worldwide.
rationale: B2B steel group supplying car makers; Austrian Grand Prix and automotive customers give hospitality value, but consumer brand use is limited.

name: EchoStar
desc: US satellite and wireless company running Hughes satellite internet, Boost Mobile, Dish TV and Sling TV services.
markets: Mainly US consumers and businesses; Hughes serves satellite broadband customers in Latin America, India and other markets.
rationale: US consumer brands Boost Mobile and Sling could use F1's growing American audience, but spectrum sales and restructuring limit spending.
changed: Acquired Dish Network in 2023; agreed spectrum sales to AT&T and SpaceX in 2025

name: GE Aerospace
desc: US maker of commercial and military jet engines, avionics and engine services for airlines, aircraft makers and armed forces.
markets: Airlines, aircraft makers and militaries worldwide, with service operations across the Americas, Europe, Middle East and Asia.
rationale: Engine technology and airline customer hospitality could suit F1, but B2B focus and defence work make sponsorship less obvious.
changed: Renamed GE Aerospace in 2024 after General Electric spun off its healthcare and energy businesses

name: General Dynamics
desc: US defence and aerospace contractor building submarines, combat vehicles, naval ships, Gulfstream business jets and government IT systems.
industry: defence contractor and business jet maker
markets: Mainly US government with allied governments in Europe and elsewhere; Gulfstream jets sold to owners worldwide.
rationale: Defence-led contractor with limited sponsorship use; only Gulfstream business jets have a plausible premium audience fit with F1.

name: Hainan Airlines
desc: Chinese airline flying scheduled domestic and international passenger services from Haikou and hubs including Beijing, Shenzhen and Xi'an.
markets: Mainly Chinese domestic passengers, plus international routes to Asia, Europe, North America and Australia.
rationale: Chinese carrier with international routes could use the Shanghai race and premium cabin marketing; limited sponsorship record since restructuring.
changed: HNA Group restructured in 2021; Liaoning Fangda Group became the strategic investor

name: Alaska Airlines
desc: US airline carrying passengers and cargo across North America and to Hawaii, with growing long-haul international routes.
markets: US, Canada, Mexico and Central America; new long-haul routes to Asia and Europe launched after the Hawaiian merger.
rationale: West Coast airline growing internationally; US races in Las Vegas and Austin offer brand and hospitality value, though focus remains domestic.
changed: Parent Alaska Air Group acquired Hawaiian Airlines in 2024

name: American Airlines
desc: US airline flying passengers and cargo to about 350 destinations from hubs including Dallas-Fort Worth, Charlotte and Miami.
markets: US domestic network plus routes to Latin America, Europe and Asia; Oneworld member.
rationale: Large US consumer brand with Miami, Austin and Las Vegas hubs or routes; F1's US growth and premium travellers make a natural fit.

name: Southwest Airlines
desc: US low-cost airline flying a Boeing 737 fleet to over 100 destinations in the US, Mexico and Caribbean.
markets: Mainly US domestic travellers, with routes to Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.
rationale: Large US consumer brand, but domestic-only network limits the value of a global F1 programme beyond US races.

name: United Airlines
desc: US airline flying passengers and cargo to more than 300 destinations on six continents from major US hubs.
markets: US domestic network plus extensive routes to Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America, Middle East and Africa; Star Alliance member.
rationale: Global network and premium business travellers suit F1 hospitality; US race growth and loyalty programme activations are clear uses.

name: International Airlines Group (IAG)
desc: Airline holding company owning British Airways, Iberia, Vueling, Aer Lingus, Level and the Avios loyalty business.
markets: European airlines flying to the Americas, Africa, Middle East and Asia from London, Madrid, Barcelona and Dublin.
rationale: British Airways and Iberia have premium customers in the UK and Spain, both F1 race hosts; strong hospitality and loyalty fit.

name: AerCap
desc: Irish aircraft leasing company that leases aircraft, engines and helicopters to airlines and operators around the world.
markets: Leases to about 300 airline customers across the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Middle East and Africa.
rationale: B2B lessor with few customers and no consumer brand; F1 hospitality could entertain airline executives, but fit is weak.
changed: Acquired GE Capital Aviation Services in 2021

name: LATAM Airlines Group
desc: Latin American airline group flying passengers and cargo through affiliates in Chile, Brazil, Peru, Colombia and Ecuador.
markets: Domestic markets in Chile, Brazil, Peru, Colombia and Ecuador, plus routes to North America, Europe and Oceania.
rationale: Strong brand in Chile and Brazil; the Sao Paulo Grand Prix gives regional marketing and hospitality opportunities.
changed: Emerged from US Chapter 11 in 2022

name: DSV
desc: Danish transport and logistics company offering air, sea and road freight plus contract logistics to business customers.
markets: Operations in about 80 countries across Europe, the Americas, Asia-Pacific, Middle East and Africa.
rationale: Global B2B logistics group; F1 freight showcase and client hospitality are plausible, though rival DHL is F1's logistics partner.
changed: Acquired DB Schenker in 2025

name: Heathrow Airport Holdings
desc: Owner and operator of London Heathrow Airport, earning charges from airlines and income from retail, parking and property.
markets: Single airport in London serving passengers and airlines from around the world; no airports outside the UK.
rationale: Huge passenger audience and UK base, but a regulated single airport with little need for global brand marketing.
changed: Ferrovial sold most of its stake to Ardian and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund in 2024

name: Vietnam Airlines
desc: Vietnamese flag carrier flying domestic and international passenger routes from Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City.
markets: Vietnam domestic network plus routes to Asia, Europe and Australia across about 19 countries; SkyTeam member.
rationale: Asian carrier with growing long-haul routes could use F1 in Asia, but state ownership and losses limit sponsorship spending.

name: gategroup
desc: Swiss provider of airline catering, onboard retail, food logistics and equipment to airlines and rail operators.
markets: Operates more than 200 facilities in over 60 countries across Europe, the Americas, Asia-Pacific and Middle East.
rationale: B2B airline supplier with little consumer brand; F1 hospitality catering could be a showcase, but sponsorship fit is weak.
changed: Acquired and delisted by HNA Group in 2016; later owned by RRJ Capital and Temasek

name: Gol Linhas Aereas
desc: Brazilian low-cost airline flying a Boeing 737 fleet on domestic routes and to South America and the Caribbean.
markets: Mainly Brazilian domestic passengers, with international routes to South America, the Caribbean and the US.
rationale: Popular Brazilian consumer brand; the Sao Paulo Grand Prix offers local marketing, but finances after restructuring limit spending.
changed: Filed for US Chapter 11 in 2024; emerged in 2025 under Abra Group

name: Virgin Atlantic
desc: British long-haul airline flying passengers and cargo from London Heathrow and Manchester to the Americas, Africa and Asia.
markets: UK travellers plus routes to North America, the Caribbean, Africa, India and Asia; SkyTeam member since 2023.
rationale: British consumer brand with premium transatlantic customers; British and US races suit brand and hospitality campaigns.

name: Grupo Aeromexico
desc: Mexican airline group operating Aeromexico on domestic routes and to the US, Latin America, Europe and Asia.
markets: Mexico domestic network plus routes to the US, Canada, Latin America, Europe and Asia; SkyTeam member.
rationale: Leading Mexican airline; the Mexico City Grand Prix and Mexican fan base offer a natural brand and hospitality fit.
changed: Emerged from US Chapter 11 in 2022; returned to public markets with a 2025 IPO

name: Delta Air Lines
desc: US airline flying passengers and cargo to destinations on six continents, with loyalty, maintenance and refinery businesses.
markets: US domestic network plus routes to Europe, Latin America, Asia-Pacific and Africa; SkyTeam founding member.
rationale: Premium US airline brand with heavy sports marketing; US races and global business travellers suit F1 hospitality.

name: Ryanair
desc: Irish ultra-low-cost airline group flying Boeing 737s to over 200 airports across Europe and North Africa.
markets: European short-haul network across about 37 countries, with some routes to Morocco and Jordan.
rationale: Very high European consumer reach, but low-fare model and cost-focused marketing make costly F1 sponsorship unlikely.

name: Azerbaijan Airlines (AZAL)
desc: State-owned flag carrier of Azerbaijan flying passengers and cargo from Baku to Europe, Asia and CIS countries.
markets: Routes from Baku to Europe, Turkey, the Middle East, Central Asia and Russia.
rationale: Azerbaijan hosts the Baku Grand Prix, giving a home-race hospitality and tourism link; small airline with limited budget.

name: ITA Airways
desc: Italian flag carrier, successor to Alitalia, flying domestic and international passenger routes from Rome Fiumicino and Milan.
markets: Italian domestic network plus routes across Europe, the Americas, Africa and Asia; Star Alliance member since 2025.
rationale: Italian flag carrier with a home race at Monza; premium travellers and Lufthansa backing support an F1 partnership.
changed: Started in 2021 as Alitalia's successor; Lufthansa bought a 41% stake in 2025

name: Riyadh Air
desc: New Saudi airline owned by the Public Investment Fund, starting international passenger flights from Riyadh with Boeing and Airbus aircraft.
markets: Launching from Riyadh to destinations worldwide, starting with London in 2025; network still building up.
rationale: New premium airline needing global awareness; Saudi Grand Prix and Gulf rivals' F1 deals make sponsorship a natural route.
changed: Founded by PIF in 2023

name: China Eastern Airlines
desc: Major Chinese airline flying domestic and international passenger and cargo routes from Shanghai Pudong and Hongqiao.
markets: Mainly Chinese domestic passengers, plus international routes across Asia, Europe, North America and Oceania; SkyTeam member.
rationale: Shanghai-based carrier for the Chinese Grand Prix; strong domestic brand but state ownership limits global sponsorship.
changed: Delisted its NYSE shares in 2022

name: Ethiopian Airlines
desc: State-owned Ethiopian flag carrier flying passengers and cargo across Africa and to Europe, Asia and the Americas.
markets: Hub in Addis Ababa serving Africa, Europe, the Middle East, Asia and the Americas; Star Alliance member.
rationale: Africa's largest airline; F1 has no African race yet, so the audience fit is limited despite global routes.

name: AirAsia
desc: Malaysian low-cost airline group flying domestic and international routes across South-East Asia, South Asia and Australia.
markets: Airlines in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and Cambodia; routes across Asia and to Australia.
rationale: Former F1 sponsor with strong South-East Asian brand; Singapore Grand Prix audience fits, though low-cost finances limit spending.
changed: Airline businesses reorganised from Capital A into AirAsia Group Berhad in 2025-26

name: Cathay Pacific Airways
desc: Hong Kong flag carrier flying passengers and cargo to destinations worldwide, also owning HK Express and Air Hong Kong.
markets: Hub in Hong Kong with routes to Asia-Pacific, Europe, North America, the Middle East and Africa.
rationale: Premium Asian airline with long-haul business travellers; Asian races and hospitality suit F1, though rivals hold airline deals.
changed: Bought back Qatar Airways' shareholding in 2024; Swire Pacific and Air China remain main shareholders

name: easyJet
desc: British low-cost airline and package holiday group flying Airbus A320-family aircraft on short-haul routes across Europe.
markets: European short-haul network across about 35 countries, plus easyJet holidays packages for UK travellers.
rationale: High European consumer awareness, but low-fare model leaves little budget for F1; European race travel packages are possible.

name: China Southern Airlines
desc: Major Chinese airline flying domestic and international passenger and cargo routes from Guangzhou and Beijing Daxing hubs.
markets: Mainly Chinese domestic passengers, plus international routes across Asia, Oceania, Europe, North America and Africa.
rationale: Large Chinese carrier; the Chinese Grand Prix offers a home link, but state ownership limits global sponsorship.
changed: Delisted its NYSE shares in 2022; left SkyTeam in 2019

name: Royal Caribbean Group
desc: Cruise holding company operating Royal Caribbean International, Celebrity Cruises and Silversea, and co-owning TUI Cruises.
markets: Cruise guests mainly from North America and Europe, with sailings worldwide and growing Asia-Pacific source markets.
rationale: Big consumer cruise brands with Miami base; Miami and Las Vegas races and premium guests suit F1, as rival MSC sponsors.
changed: Renamed from Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd. in 2020

name: Airbnb
desc: Online marketplace for short- and long-term home rentals and experiences, charging service fees to guests and hosts.
markets: Listings and guests in more than 220 countries and regions, mainly North America, Europe and Latin America.
rationale: Global consumer travel brand; race-week stays and local experiences give a direct F1 activation and marketing use.

name: Avolta
desc: Swiss travel retailer operating duty-free shops, convenience stores and restaurants in airports, stations, motorways and cruise ships.
markets: Operates in over 75 countries across Europe, North America, Latin America, Middle East and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: B2B and travel-retail group with brand partners; F1 hospitality could suit landlord and supplier relations, but consumer brand is weak.
changed: Formed from the 2023 merger of Dufry and Autogrill

name: Expedia Group
desc: Online travel company operating Expedia, Hotels.com, Vrbo and other booking sites, plus B2B travel distribution services.
markets: Travellers and partners in North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America; strongest in the US.
rationale: Global consumer travel brands; race-trip packages and US fan growth make F1 a plausible marketing platform.

name: Hertz Global Holdings
desc: US car rental company operating the Hertz, Dollar, Thrifty and Firefly brands at airports and local branches.
markets: Mainly North America and Europe, with franchised locations in Asia-Pacific, Latin America, Middle East and Africa.
rationale: Well-known travel brand with motorsport history; US races suit marketing, but recent losses limit sponsorship budgets.
changed: Emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2021

name: Carnival Corporation
desc: Cruise company operating Carnival, Princess, Holland America, P&O Cruises, Cunard, Costa, AIDA and Seabourn brands.
markets: Guests mainly from North America, the UK, Germany, Italy and Australia, with cruises worldwide.
rationale: Mass-market and premium cruise brands across the US and Europe; F1 could support premium brands, as rival MSC sponsors F1.
changed: Ended its dual-listed structure with Carnival plc in May 2026

name: OYO
desc: Indian hospitality technology company that brands and manages budget hotels and holiday homes through its booking platform.
markets: Mainly India, South-East Asia, Europe (Belvilla vacation homes) and the US (Motel 6 and Studio 6).
rationale: Budget hotel brand in India and the US; F1 audience fit is moderate and finances favour performance marketing over sponsorship.
changed: Bought Motel 6 owner G6 Hospitality in 2024; parent Oravel Stays renamed PRISM in 2025

name: Booking Holdings
desc: Online travel company owning Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, Kayak and OpenTable, earning booking commissions and advertising fees.
markets: Travellers and accommodation partners in about 220 countries, strongest in Europe, North America and Asia.
rationale: Large global advertiser in travel; race-trip accommodation and global audience make F1 an obvious marketing fit.

name: Sandals Resorts International
desc: Jamaican operator of all-inclusive Caribbean resorts under the Sandals couples and Beaches family brands.
markets: Resorts across Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Antigua, Bahamas, Barbados, Grenada and other Caribbean islands; guests mainly from the US, Canada and UK.
rationale: Strong US and UK consumer marketing; Miami Grand Prix could suit a Caribbean resort brand, though budget is limited.

name: Abercrombie & Kent
desc: Luxury travel company organising tailor-made journeys, safaris, small-group tours and expedition cruises for affluent travellers.
markets: Clients mainly from North America, the UK and Australia, with trips and local offices in over 100 countries.
rationale: Affluent clientele overlaps with F1 hospitality buyers; race-weekend luxury packages are plausible, but marketing budgets are small.

name: American Express Global Business Travel
desc: Corporate travel management company providing booking, expense and meetings services to businesses, trading as Amex GBT.
markets: Corporate clients in more than 140 countries across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
rationale: B2B travel manager for large companies; F1 hospitality could serve clients, and the Amex brand already partners with F1.
changed: Listed via SPAC merger in 2022; acquired CWT in 2025

name: Transat A.T.
desc: Canadian leisure travel group selling flights and holiday packages through Air Transat and Transat tour operations.
markets: Canadian travellers flying to Europe, the Caribbean, Mexico and the US; sales offices in Canada and France.
rationale: Quebec-centred consumer brand; the Canadian Grand Prix in Montreal offers a local fit, but finances are stretched.

name: Travelport
desc: Travel technology company running a global distribution system that connects airlines, hotels and car rental firms with travel agencies.
markets: Travel agencies and suppliers worldwide across Europe, the Americas, Asia-Pacific and Middle East.
rationale: B2B travel platform with no consumer brand; F1 hospitality for agency clients is possible but the fit is weak.
changed: Taken private by Siris Capital and Elliott in 2019

name: Las Vegas Sands
desc: Developer and operator of integrated casino resorts including Marina Bay Sands in Singapore and Venetian Macao.
markets: Resorts in Macau and Singapore only; no US casinos since selling its Las Vegas properties in 2022.
rationale: Marina Bay Sands overlooks the Singapore Grand Prix circuit; strong hospitality fit, but gambling rules limit some markets.
changed: Sold The Venetian and Palazzo in Las Vegas in 2022

name: Melco Resorts & Entertainment
desc: Developer and operator of integrated casino resorts in Macau, Manila and Cyprus, including City of Dreams and Studio City.
markets: Resorts in Macau, the Philippines and Cyprus; customers mainly from mainland China and Asia.
rationale: Asian casino resort brand with premium guests; F1 hospitality fits, but gambling restrictions limit sponsorship use.
changed: Renamed from Melco Crown Entertainment in 2017

name: Tripadvisor
desc: Travel platform offering user reviews and bookings for hotels, tours and restaurants through Tripadvisor, Viator and TheFork.
markets: Users and partners across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific; TheFork strongest in Europe.
rationale: Global consumer travel brand; race-weekend experiences via Viator are a plausible F1 tie-in, though budgets are modest.
changed: Merged with Liberty TripAdvisor Holdings in 2025

name: Fosun Tourism Group (FOLIDAY)
desc: Chinese leisure group owning Club Med resorts, Atlantis Sanya and the Thomas Cook brand, selling holidays and resort stays.
markets: Club Med resorts in Europe, Asia, the Americas and Africa; Atlantis Sanya and travel services in China.
rationale: Club Med is a recognised European and Asian leisure brand; F1 could support premium holidays, though the fit is moderate.
changed: Fosun bought Club Med in 2015 and the Thomas Cook brand in 2019

name: Viking Holdings
desc: Cruise company operating river, ocean and expedition cruises for older affluent travellers under the Viking brand.
markets: Guests mainly from the US, Canada, UK and Australia; cruises in Europe, Egypt, Asia and the Americas.
rationale: Affluent older customers are a weak fit with F1's younger audience; brand prefers cultural sponsorships such as PBS Masterpiece.
changed: Listed on the NYSE in 2024

name: Royal Caribbean Group
desc: Cruise holding company operating Royal Caribbean International, Celebrity Cruises and Silversea, and co-owning TUI Cruises.
markets: Cruise guests mainly from North America and Europe, with sailings worldwide and growing Asia-Pacific source markets.
rationale: Big consumer cruise brands with Miami base; Miami and Las Vegas races and premium guests suit F1, as rival MSC sponsors.
changed: Renamed Royal Caribbean Group in 2020

name: Virgin Voyages
desc: Adults-only cruise line offering voyages from Miami, the Mediterranean and other ports on four Virgin-branded ships.
markets: Guests mainly from the US and UK; sailings in the Caribbean, Mediterranean and Northern Europe.
rationale: Lifestyle cruise brand with younger adult guests; Miami base and Virgin marketing style suit F1 events and activations.

name: Trip.com Group
desc: Online travel company operating Ctrip, Trip.com, Skyscanner and Qunar, selling flights, hotels, rail tickets and packages.
markets: Mainly mainland China, with Trip.com and Skyscanner serving travellers across Asia, Europe and other markets.
rationale: Growing international travel brand with sports sponsorship; Asian races and global expansion make F1 a strong fit.
changed: Renamed from Ctrip.com International in 2019

name: Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts
desc: Canadian luxury hotel company managing more than 130 hotels, resorts and branded residences worldwide.
markets: Hotels in North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America.
rationale: Luxury brand with high-net-worth guests; race-city hotels and F1 hospitality offer a strong premium fit.
changed: Cascade Investment raised its stake to 71.25% in 2022, with Kingdom Holding owning 23.75%

name: Minor Hotels
desc: Hotel owner and operator running Anantara, Avani, NH, nhow, Tivoli, Oaks and Elewana hotels and resorts.
markets: More than 550 hotels in over 55 countries across Asia-Pacific, Europe, Middle East, Africa and the Americas.
rationale: Large hotel group in many race cities, especially in Europe through NH; hospitality and brand awareness fit F1.
changed: Parent took control of NH Hotel Group in 2018

name: Shangri-La Asia
desc: Hong Kong-based luxury hotel group operating Shangri-La, Kerry, JEN and Traders hotels and resorts.
markets: Hotels mainly in mainland China and Asia-Pacific, with some in the Middle East, Europe and North America.
rationale: Asian luxury hotel brand with properties in race cities such as Singapore and Shanghai; premium hospitality fits F1.

name: Trip.com
desc: International online travel booking brand of Trip.com Group, selling flights, hotels, trains, car rentals and attraction tickets.
markets: Travellers across Asia, Europe, the Middle East and other markets outside mainland China.
rationale: International travel brand seeking awareness outside China; Asian and European races make F1 a strong marketing fit.

name: Qantas
desc: Australian flag carrier operating Qantas, QantasLink and Jetstar passenger services plus Qantas Freight and a loyalty programme.
markets: Australian domestic network plus routes to Asia, North America, Europe, New Zealand and the Pacific.
rationale: Very strong Australian brand; the Melbourne Grand Prix and loyalty members suit F1 hospitality and marketing.

name: Wingstop
desc: US franchisor of fast-casual chicken wing restaurants, earning royalties and fees from franchised and company-owned outlets.
markets: Mainly US restaurants, with franchised outlets in the UK, Mexico, the Middle East and other countries.
rationale: US consumer brand with sports marketing; F1's young US audience fits, though international scale is still small.

name: TUI Group
desc: German leisure travel group combining tour operators, TUI fly airlines, hotels, cruise lines and a tours and activities platform.
markets: Customers mainly in Germany, the UK, the Nordics and Benelux, with hotels and cruises worldwide.
rationale: Major European consumer travel brand; race-travel packages and holiday marketing in Germany and the UK fit F1 audiences.
changed: Moved its main listing from London to Frankfurt in 2024

name: DraftKings
desc: US online sports betting, iGaming, daily fantasy sports and lottery company operating apps in legal US states and Ontario.
markets: Customers in legal US states and Ontario, Canada; no other international operations.
rationale: Heavy US sports advertiser; F1's US growth fits, as rival FanDuel is an F1 partner, though betting rules restrict some activations.
changed: Acquired lottery app Jackpocket in 2024

name: Aristocrat Technologies
desc: Gaming business of Aristocrat Leisure, making casino slot machines, gaming systems and digital casino games.
markets: Casino operators in the Americas, Australia, Europe and Asia, plus mobile game players worldwide.
rationale: B2B gaming supplier with casino customers; Las Vegas race hospitality is plausible, but gambling links limit sponsorship use.

name: Superbet
desc: Romanian sports betting and gaming group running online betting, online casino and retail betting shops.
markets: Romania, Poland, Serbia, Belgium and Brazil; expanding into new regulated markets.
rationale: Heavy sports sponsor seeking awareness in new markets; F1 fits, but gambling advertising limits restrict activations.

name: FDJ United
desc: French lottery and gaming group operating France's and Ireland's national lotteries, sports betting and online gaming brands.
markets: France and Ireland lotteries, with Kindred's Unibet online betting in Europe.
rationale: Large French consumer brand and cycling sponsor; F1 is plausible for Unibet, but French gambling advertising rules limit use.
changed: Acquired Kindred Group in 2024; renamed FDJ United in 2025

name: Sportradar
desc: Sports data and technology company supplying live data, odds, streaming and integrity services to bookmakers, media and leagues.
markets: Betting operators, media and sports federations in over 100 countries, with major US league rights.
rationale: B2B sports data supplier; F1 data or integrity tie-in is a technology showcase, though rival ALT Sports Data partners F1.

name: LIV Golf
desc: Saudi-funded professional golf league that ran team-based tournaments with star players between 2022 and 2026.
markets: Events were held in the US, Europe, Asia, Australia and the Middle East; the tour has ended.
rationale: Tour no longer operates; PIF-funded sports property with no brand to market through F1.
changed: Wikipedia records the tour as operating only from 2022 to 2026

name: PureGym
desc: British low-cost gym chain offering no-contract memberships at more than 500 clubs in the UK and abroad.
markets: UK, Denmark, Switzerland, the UAE and other countries, plus US clubs after buying Blink Fitness.
rationale: Large UK consumer brand; F1 fitness content could suit marketing, but low-cost model limits sponsorship budgets.
changed: Bought US gym chain Blink Fitness out of bankruptcy in 2024

name: Equinox Group
desc: US luxury fitness company running Equinox clubs, SoulCycle studios and Equinox Hotels for premium members.
markets: Mainly major US cities, with clubs in London, Toronto and Vancouver.
rationale: Premium lifestyle brand with affluent members; F1 performance and wellness content fits, especially around US races.
changed: Its Blink Fitness unit filed for bankruptcy and was sold in 2024

name: Real Madrid C.F.
desc: Spanish professional football and basketball club earning revenue from broadcasting, matchday, sponsorship and merchandise.
markets: Spanish club with a worldwide fan base and commercial partners across Europe, the Americas, Middle East and Asia.
rationale: Itself a sports property selling sponsorship; Madrid Grand Prix from 2026 offers cross-promotion, but it is not a buyer.

name: Chelsea Football Club
desc: English Premier League football club earning revenue from broadcasting, matchday ticketing, sponsorship and merchandise.
markets: London club with a global fan base, notably in Asia, the US and Africa.
rationale: A sports property that sells sponsorship rather than buys it; F1 cross-promotion is possible but weak.
changed: Bought in 2022 by the BlueCo consortium led by Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital

name: Inter Milan
desc: Italian Serie A football club earning revenue from broadcasting, matchday, sponsorship and merchandise.
markets: Milan club with fans across Italy, Europe, Asia and the Americas.
rationale: A sports property that sells sponsorship rather than buys it; Monza Grand Prix cross-promotion is possible but weak.
changed: Oaktree Capital took ownership from Suning Holdings in 2024

name: FC Bayern Munchen
desc: German football club, owned mainly by its members, earning revenue from broadcasting, matchday, sponsorship and merchandise.
markets: German club with a global fan base and offices in the US and China.
rationale: A sports property that sells sponsorship rather than buys it; shareholder Audi's F1 entry offers cross-promotion only.

name: Sotheby's
desc: International auction house selling fine art, jewellery, watches, wine, cars and collectibles to private collectors.
markets: About 80 locations in 40 countries, with main salerooms in New York, London, Paris and Hong Kong.
rationale: Wealthy collector clientele overlaps with F1 Paddock Club buyers; car auctions and hospitality give a plausible premium fit.
changed: Taken private by Patrick Drahi in 2019; ADIA bought a minority stake in 2024

name: Umicore
desc: Belgian materials technology group making emission catalysts, battery materials and recycling precious metals for industrial customers.
industry: catalysts, battery materials and metals recycling
markets: Plants and customers in Europe, Asia and the Americas, supplying car makers and battery producers.
rationale: B2B supplier to car makers; sustainable-materials story could suit F1, but limited consumer brand and battery losses weaken fit.

name: Alpargatas
desc: Brazilian footwear company that makes and sells Havaianas rubber flip-flops and sandals in Brazil and abroad.
markets: Mainly Brazil, with Havaianas sold in over 100 countries across Europe, the US and Asia.
rationale: Havaianas is a global lifestyle brand; the Sao Paulo Grand Prix and summer campaigns are possible, but fit is moderate.

name: Orkla
desc: Norwegian consumer goods group making packaged foods, snacks, confectionery, personal care and health products.
markets: Mainly the Nordics and Baltics, with operations in Central Europe and India.
rationale: Regional food brands focused on Nordic shoppers; F1 adds little reach, so the fit is weak.

name: Dream Games
desc: Turkish mobile game studio that develops Royal Match and Royal Kingdom, earning from in-app purchases.
markets: Players worldwide, mainly in the US, Europe and Asia.
rationale: Top-grossing mobile game with large user-acquisition spend; F1 audience could support brand campaigns.
changed: Acquired by Savvy Games Group in 2025

name: Entain
desc: International sports betting and gaming group owning Ladbrokes, Coral, bwin, Sportingbet and PartyPoker, and half of BetMGM.
markets: UK, Europe, Australia, New Zealand, Brazil and the US through the BetMGM joint venture.
rationale: Big sports betting advertiser; F1 fits, but gambling advertising rules in key markets restrict activations.
changed: Renamed from GVC Holdings in 2020

name: Vantage Studios
desc: Ubisoft subsidiary that develops and runs the Assassin's Creed, Far Cry and Rainbow Six video game franchises.
markets: Players worldwide across North America, Europe and Asia through digital and retail sales.
rationale: Major game franchises reach young global audiences; in-game or esports tie-ins with F1 are plausible.
changed: Created by Ubisoft in 2025; Tencent agreed to invest about EUR 1.16bn for a minority stake

name: Light & Wonder
desc: US gaming company making slot machines, table games, casino systems, online casino content and social casino games.
markets: Casino operators and online gaming customers in the Americas, Europe, Australia and Asia.
rationale: B2B casino supplier; Las Vegas Grand Prix hospitality is plausible, but consumer brand and gambling ties limit fit.
changed: Renamed from Scientific Games in 2022; bought out SciPlay minority shareholders in 2023

name: Fanatics
desc: US sports platform selling licensed fan merchandise, trading cards and collectibles, and running sports betting and live events.
markets: Mainly the US, with merchandise operations for leagues and clubs in Europe and other regions.
rationale: Already sells F1 merchandise; deeper F1 partnership could expand fan commerce and betting in the US.
f1: Operates Formula 1's official online store under a merchandise partnership with F1

name: Epic Games
desc: US video game and software company behind Fortnite, Unreal Engine and the Epic Games Store.
markets: Players and developers worldwide; Unreal Engine also used in film, automotive and simulation.
rationale: Fortnite reaches young global gamers and Unreal Engine powers car design; in-game and technology tie-ins suit F1.

name: Square Enix
desc: European arm of Japanese game publisher Square Enix, publishing Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest and Kingdom Hearts games.
markets: Group sells games in Japan, North America, Europe and Asia; London office covers Europe.
rationale: Global game franchises with young audiences; F1 tie-ins are possible but not obvious.
changed: Sold Eidos and Crystal Dynamics to Embracer in 2022

name: Nexon
desc: US arm of Nexon, publishing online live-service games such as MapleStory, The First Descendant and Blue Archive.
markets: Group revenue mainly from South Korea, China, Japan and North America.
rationale: Online gaming brand with young audiences; racing games such as KartRider give a possible F1 tie-in.

name: Hybe
desc: South Korean entertainment company managing K-pop artists such as BTS and Seventeen and running the Weverse fan platform.
markets: Korea, Japan, the US and other markets, with labels in Korea, Japan, the US and Latin America.
rationale: Global youth fan base; music and artist collaborations with F1 are plausible, but it sells rather than buys sponsorship.
changed: Renamed from Big Hit Entertainment in 2021

name: Tesla
desc: US maker of electric cars, battery storage and solar products, also developing self-driving software and humanoid robots.
industry: electric vehicle and energy storage maker
markets: Sells vehicles and energy products across North America, Europe, China and Asia-Pacific; factories in the US, China and Germany.
rationale: Car maker with rivals in F1, but Tesla avoids paid sponsorship and traditional advertising; fit is weak.

name: DoorDash
desc: Online delivery platform connecting consumers with restaurants, grocery and retail stores for delivery and pickup.
markets: US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and Europe through Wolt, plus the UK and Middle East through Deliveroo.
rationale: Large consumer brand expanding internationally; F1 events and fan delivery offers are plausible marketing uses.
changed: Acquired Wolt in 2022 and Deliveroo in 2025

name: GE HealthCare
desc: Medical technology company making imaging scanners, ultrasound, patient monitoring equipment, contrast agents and healthcare software.
markets: Hospitals and clinics in more than 160 countries across the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
rationale: B2B medical technology brand; F1 data and performance themes give limited marketing value to hospital buyers.
changed: Spun off from General Electric in 2023

name: JD.com
desc: Chinese e-commerce and retail company selling electronics, groceries and general goods online with its own logistics network.
markets: Mainly mainland China, with growing logistics and retail operations in Europe and other international markets.
rationale: Chinese consumer giant expanding abroad; the Chinese Grand Prix and international expansion make F1 a plausible platform.
